families.outcome: Interpret a speed-time graph for motion in a straight line: read a value, find a gradient, recognise the nature of the motion, and find distance from the area
families.context: One inline-SVG speed-time graph of a bus: 0 to 12 m/s over 4 s, steady for 4 s, back to rest over 4 s

variants.variation: read a value off the sloping section, where the answer is not a plotted vertex
variants.misconception: reads the time axis instead of the speed axis, or gives the graph's peak value

variants.variation: find the gradient of one named section rather than read a point
variants.misconception: divides the speed change by the total journey time instead of by the time it was changing

variants.variation: diagnose a stated pupil claim about the flat section rather than describe the graph
variants.misconception: carries the distance-time rule across: a flat line read as 'at rest' on a speed axis

variants.variation: area under the graph, split into three shapes; nothing can be read directly
variants.misconception: multiplies the maximum speed by the total time, counting the sloping parts as full speed

variants.variation: evaluate a driver's claim about average speed; requires computing the area first, then judging
variants.misconception: takes the speed held longest, or the midpoint of first and last speed, as the average

families.outcome: Solve problems on the motion of objects, converting to SI units before calculating
families.context: Journeys on Mauritian roads with the quantities deliberately supplied in km and minutes

variants.variation: two conversions needed before one division; the unconverted results are the distractors
variants.misconception: divides before converting (3.6/4 = 0.9), or converts the distance only (3600/4 = 900)

variants.variation: reversed: speed and time given, distance wanted, and the ANSWER unit differs from the working unit
variants.misconception: multiplies m/s by minutes, then forgets to convert the answer from metres to km

variants.variation: time is the unknown, and a conversion is needed at both ends of the calculation
variants.misconception: divides kilometres by metres per second and answers 1.2

variants.variation: compare two routes under a constraint; the shorter route is the slower one
variants.misconception: assumes the shorter route must be quicker; or compares unconverted quotients, giving a 0.1 'saving'

variants.variation: diagnose what is wrong with a correct calculation that is wrongly described
variants.misconception: treats an average speed as the speed at a particular instant

families.outcome: Use an appropriate instrument for a length, convert to SI units, and compare the accuracy of simple instruments
families.context: Finding the thickness of one sheet of paper by measuring a stack of them

variants.variation: divide a measured total to get the value for one item
variants.misconception: divides the wrong way round, making one sheet thicker than the whole stack

variants.variation: convert a sub-millimetre length to metres; every distractor is one wrong power of ten
variants.misconception: divides by 100 (the centimetre factor) or by 10, or relabels the number unchanged

variants.variation: justify the method rather than execute it; requires knowing what the instrument can resolve
variants.misconception: believes an instrument can measure anything if you look carefully enough

variants.variation: compare two pupils' methods that give the same value, and decide which value is more reliable
variants.misconception: the same instrument must give the same reliability, whatever is measured with it

variants.variation: produce the resolution of an instrument instead of selecting it
variants.misconception: gives the ruler's greatest length (30 cm) when asked for the smallest it can measure

families.outcome: Recognise a zero (end) error and correct readings for it
families.context: Top-pan balances carrying a known zero error, used forwards, backwards and in a difference

variants.variation: correct a single reading for a NEGATIVE zero error, so the correction is an addition
variants.misconception: always subtracts the zero error, whatever its sign

variants.variation: reversed: a known standard mass is used to find the instrument's fault
variants.misconception: adds the two masses, or reports the reading as though it were the error

variants.variation: judge whether a correction is needed at all when the result is a DIFFERENCE of two readings
variants.misconception: a known error must always be applied; a fixed offset in fact cancels in a subtraction

variants.variation: correct once, then share out; the order of the two operations is the whole question
variants.misconception: corrects after dividing, or applies the zero error once per marble

families.outcome: Recall and use Q = It and W = QV
families.context: Lamps and torch bulbs run for a time given in minutes, so every part needs a conversion to seconds

variants.variation: direct Q = It with the time supplied in minutes
variants.misconception: uses the time in minutes, giving an answer 60 times too small

variants.variation: reversed: charge given, current wanted
variants.misconception: divides by 5 instead of 300, producing a current no household circuit could carry

variants.variation: chains the two named formulae: Q = It feeds W = QV
variants.misconception: multiplies all three given numbers once, with the time still in minutes

variants.variation: apparent contradiction: very different current and voltage, identical energy transferred
variants.misconception: judges energy by the current alone, or by the voltage alone, instead of the product

variants.variation: produce the unit of charge that defines the volt, rather than select it
variants.misconception: answers 'ampere', confusing the unit of current with the unit of charge

families.outcome: Solve problems on simple DC series circuits
families.context: One inline-SVG series circuit, 4 ohm and 8 ohm resistors on a 12 V supply, then one component swapped

variants.variation: combine two series resistances
variants.misconception: averages the two resistances instead of adding them

variants.variation: two steps: total resistance, then I = V/R
variants.misconception: uses one resistor's value as though it were the whole circuit's resistance

variants.variation: three steps, ending with V = IR applied to ONE component
variants.misconception: shares the supply p.d. equally between the two components and answers 6 V

variants.variation: change one condition and predict the effect on TWO coupled quantities; answers are relative, not numeric
variants.misconception: a component whose own resistance has not changed must keep the same p.d. across it

families.outcome: Apply the laws of reflection; measure angles from the normal; explain diffuse reflection
families.context: One inline-SVG plane mirror with a single incident ray, labelled 30 degrees to the mirror SURFACE

variants.variation: convert an angle given from the surface into the angle of incidence
variants.misconception: measures the angle from the mirror instead of from the normal and answers 30

variants.variation: same figure, but the angle wanted spans both rays and the normal between them
variants.misconception: gives the angle of reflection (60) as though it were the angle between the two rays

variants.variation: produce the name of the reference line rather than pick it from a list
variants.misconception: answers 'perpendicular' or 'vertical', confusing the line's name with its direction

variants.variation: resolve an apparent contradiction: the laws seem to fail on a rough wall
variants.misconception: a law that does not give the familiar result must have stopped applying

families.outcome: Compare the advantages and drawbacks of electricity sources and justify a choice from data
families.context: One table of three supplies for a village (output, fuel cost, pollution) against a stated daily and night-time demand

variants.variation: read the table and apply a threshold before comparing on cost
variants.misconception: compares on cost alone and picks the cheapest row without checking it meets the demand

variants.variation: a daily total that looks sufficient conceals WHEN the energy arrives
variants.misconception: compares daily totals (450 vs 400) and concludes there is no shortfall

variants.variation: evaluate a councillor's claim whose premises are all true but whose conclusion fails
variants.misconception: treats a correct daily total as a guarantee of supply at every hour

variants.variation: identify the MISSING information; two distractors are already in the table and one is irrelevant
variants.misconception: decides from whatever data is present without asking what the decision actually requires

families.outcome: Solve problems on conservation of energy in simple systems (falling objects)
families.context: Objects dropped from a height: a ball, a bouncing ball, then a marble against a sheet of paper

variants.variation: name the direction of the transfer during the fall
variants.misconception: reverses the two stores, which describes an object thrown upwards instead

variants.variation: explain why the outcome falls short of what conservation alone would predict
variants.misconception: energy is 'used up' or destroyed at the bounce, rather than transferred elsewhere

variants.variation: apparent contradiction: the same paper, unchanged in mass, falls differently once crumpled
variants.misconception: heavier objects always fall faster; here only the area facing the air changed

variants.variation: produce the name of the store that is FILLING, not the one emptying
variants.misconception: names the gravitational store, which is the one being emptied

families.outcome: Process, interpret and evaluate results, and record data in a properly headed table
families.context: One table of spring lengths against load, whose last reading breaks the proportion and was repeated three times

variants.variation: derive extension from lengths; the table does not contain the answer
variants.misconception: reads the length straight off the table and gives 26.0 cm as the extension

variants.variation: predict a value between two rows using the pattern, not the printed numbers
variants.misconception: interpolates the LENGTH instead of the extension, or forgets to subtract the unloaded length

variants.variation: judge whether a claimed proportionality actually holds across the whole data set
variants.misconception: any set of rising readings shows proportionality; or the odd point 'must be a mistake' (it was repeated three times)

variants.variation: redeems the audit's seed g9s-inq-350 by PRODUCING the missing element of a heading, not selecting it
variants.misconception: writes the unit beside every number in the column instead of once in the heading

families.outcome: Distinguish distance from displacement and speed from velocity for a real journey
families.context: One inline-SVG plan of an 80 m by 60 m field, walked round from a marked corner

variants.variation: total path length round a closed shape
variants.misconception: adds only the two labelled sides and answers 140 m

variants.variation: same journey, the other quantity; the answer is zero
variants.misconception: assumes displacement must equal the distance walked

variants.variation: both quantities at once, as rates, for a journey that clearly happened yet has zero velocity
variants.misconception: treats speed and velocity as interchangeable words for the same thing

variants.variation: compare two walkers where the faster one has the SMALLER average velocity
variants.misconception: whoever has the greater speed must also have the greater velocity

families.outcome: Measure current with an ammeter and voltage with a voltmeter; understand p.d. in a series circuit
families.context: Meters placed on series circuits, and a measured result that contradicts a pupil's prediction

variants.variation: choose how BOTH meters are connected in one decision
variants.misconception: swaps them, which short-circuits the lamp with the ammeter and nearly stops the current with the voltmeter

variants.variation: explain why a measured result differs from a stated prediction
variants.misconception: current is 'used up' by the lamps; it is energy that is used up, not charge

variants.variation: calculate the remaining p.d., then infer a property of the component from it
variants.misconception: the supply is always shared equally, or the full supply p.d. appears across each lamp

variants.variation: produce the instrument's name from what it measures and how it is connected
variants.misconception: answers 'ammeter', which measures current and goes in series

families.outcome: Define and calculate acceleration for motion in a straight line
families.context: Vehicles speeding up and braking on a straight road

variants.variation: acceleration from a non-zero starting speed
variants.misconception: divides the FINAL speed by the time, ignoring that the lorry was already moving

variants.variation: reversed: acceleration given, time wanted
variants.misconception: multiplies instead of dividing, giving an implausible 50 s stopping time

variants.variation: interpret the SIGN of a recorded acceleration against a stated direction of travel
variants.misconception: reads a minus sign as 'moving backwards' rather than 'slowing down'

variants.variation: compare two accelerations engineered to have the SAME change in speed
variants.misconception: compares the change in speed alone, or the final speed, and ignores the time
